title: Reading Luke and Acts

objectives.can: Read Luke's more literary Greek: longer periods, participles, the optative and a larger vocabulary.

explanation.summary: Luke and Acts are the work of one author, and they show a wider range of Greek than any other part of the Gospels: a polished opening sentence, long chains of participles, an optative mood that other books rarely use, and, in Luke 1–2, a deliberately biblical style. This lesson describes those features and sends you into Paul's speech in Athens.

sections.heading: A literary opening sentence
body: Luke 1:1–4 is a single long sentence, a period. It begins with ἐπειδήπερ, 'since', and does not reach its main verb until the third verse: ἔδοξε in 1:3. Verses 1 and 2 are the 'since' clause, in which many have undertaken to set down an account; 1:3 gives the author's decision; 1:4 gives his purpose with ἵνα.

Notice how the sentence is built. The decision, ἔδοξε κἀμοὶ … γράψαι, is 'it seemed good also to me to write', with the dative κἀμοί, 'also to me', and an infinitive for what was decided. Between them stands a perfect participle in the dative, παρηκολουθηκότι, agreeing with κἀμοί, followed by a string of adverbs: ἄνωθεν, ἀκριβῶς, καθεξῆς. This is the style of a formal preface, and readers have often compared it with the prefaces of Greek historians and other writers.

sections.heading: Participles and long sentences
body: In both books Luke often builds sentences by placing participles around a main verb, and his sentences are usually more heavily subordinated than Mark's. In Acts 17:30 the participle ὑπεριδών, 'having overlooked', comes before the main verb παραγγέλλει, and in 17:31 two aorist participles, παρασχών and ἀναστήσας, close the sentence. The reading skill is the one from Stage 5: find the finite verb first, then fit each participle to it.
You also meet genitive absolutes, infinitives of purpose or result, and indirect questions. These are the tools of a writer who subordinates his clauses, where Mark joins them with καί.

sections.heading: The biblical style of Luke 1–2
body: After the polished preface Luke changes register. Luke 1:5 begins Ἐγένετο ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις Ἡρῴδου, and 1:8 begins Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ ἱερατεύειν αὐτόν, where ἐγένετο with ἐν τῷ and an infinitive introduces a time. Grammarians commonly describe this ἐγένετο construction as a feature of the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, and say that Luke is imitating that style in the opening chapters; the narrative also has the clause-after-clause rhythm of the Septuagint.

Whatever the explanation (and it is a matter of discussion whether Luke imitates the Septuagint, draws on Semitic sources, or both), the effect for the reader is clear: the preface of 1:1–4 and the narrative of 1:5 are different registers within the same book.

sections.heading: The optative
body: The optative mood is rare in the New Testament. In the analysed text, Luke and Acts together hold 28 of its 68 optative forms. Two uses are common in these books. The first is a wish: γένοιτό μοι in Luke 1:38, 'may it happen to me'. The second is the optative in an indirect question after a past tense, as in Luke 1:29, where Mary 'wondered what sort of greeting this might be' (ποταπὸς εἴη ὁ ἀσπασμὸς οὗτος).

Acts 17:27 has two optatives together, ψηλαφήσειαν and εὕροιεν, after εἰ ἄρα γε, giving the hoped-for result of seeking God: 'if perhaps they might feel their way to him and find him'. The optative gives such statements a tentative, possible character. Do not try to give it a single English equivalent; read the optative as 'might' or 'may' and look at the clause it stands in.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read Acts 17:22–31 for its plan: Paul addresses the Athenians (Ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι), builds on an inscription, speaks of God as maker, and ends with a call to change and a day of judgement. Then look at the grammar. The speech has relative clauses, participles, an optative, a quoted phrase from a poet in 17:28, and μὲν οὖν in 17:30. Take it a sentence at a time; the longest sentences have only one main verb.

misunderstandings: Taking every optative as a wish. In Luke and Acts it also appears in indirect questions, as in Luke 1:29, and in clauses like Acts 17:27.
Looking for the main verb of Luke 1:1 in verse 1. The first verse is a subordinate clause; the main verb ἔδοξε waits until 1:3.
Reading ἐγένετο in Luke 1:5 as 'became' or 'was made'. Here it opens the narrative and means roughly 'it happened'.
Assuming Luke's Greek is of one kind. The preface, the Septuagintal narrative of Luke 1–2 and a speech in Acts differ in register.

deeper.heading: One author, several voices
body: Readers have often described Luke as the New Testament writer best able to change style: periodic in the preface, biblical in the infancy narratives, closer to educated speech in parts of Acts. How deliberate this is, and how much comes from his sources, is argued about. The grammar shows the difference in sentence shape; it cannot decide the reason.

examples.analysis: Ἐπειδήπερ opens a long 'since' clause. ἐπεχείρησαν is an aorist indicative with an infinitive, ἀνατάξασθαι: 'they undertook to set down'. πεπληροφορημένων is a perfect passive participle describing the matters. The sentence has no main verb yet.

examples.analysis: ἔδοξε is the main verb of the whole opening sentence. κἀμοί is καὶ ἐμοί, 'also to me', and γράψαι, an infinitive, says what seemed good. παρηκολουθηκότι is a perfect participle agreeing with κἀμοί; ἀκριβῶς and καθεξῆς are adverbs. κράτιστε Θεόφιλε is the address.

options: A relative clause; the main clause is in 1:2

practice.explain: Ἐπειδήπερ means 'since', and the sentence runs on through verse 2 to ἔδοξε in verse 3. The ἵνα clause of verse 4 gives the purpose.

options: May it happen to me according to your word
It happened to me according to your word
It will happen to you according to my word
Did it happen to me according to your word?
check.explain: γένοιτο is an aorist optative; standing alone as the verb of a main clause, it is an optative of wish. μοι is the dative 'to me' and σου is genitive 'your'.

options: A world that has no day
A day on which he judged the inhabited world
A day on which he is about to judge the inhabited world
A day that the world must judge
check.explain: μέλλει with an infinitive, κρίνειν, means 'is about to' or 'is going to'. ἐν ᾗ is a relative phrase 'on which', agreeing with ἡμέραν.

reading.why: Ten verses of one speech that show Luke's subordinating style: relative clauses, participles stacked before the main verb, an optative in 17:27, an infinitive-with-μέλλει construction in 17:31, and a quoted phrase in 17:28.
